summary: Describes the Optimized Link State Routing (OLSR) protocol for mobile ad hoc networks. It tailors classical link-state routing to wireless networks by using multipoint relays, selected nodes that forward broadcast messages, to reduce flooding overhead. The RFC is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: In a big crowd, shouting everything to everyone is noisy. Here, a few chosen friends repeat the news, so everyone hears it with far less shouting. It helps phones and radios find paths without towers.

subtitle: A proactive link-state routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks that floods through a few chosen relay nodes.

tldr.problem: In a mobile wireless network with no fixed infrastructure, classical link-state flooding makes every node retransmit every message, which creates heavy overhead.
tldr.mechanism: Each node picks a small set of symmetric neighbors as multipoint relays (MPRs). Only MPRs retransmit its broadcasts and only MPRs generate topology information, and nodes use that partial link-state data to compute shortest-hop routes.
tldr.outcome: OLSR cuts control traffic substantially and provides optimal routes in terms of hop count, and the RFC says it suits large, dense networks. The RFC is Experimental and specifies no security measures of its own.

today: RFC 3626 is an Experimental RFC, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says OLSR specifies no special security measures.

sections.title: What OLSR Is
sections.content:
The Optimized Link State Routing Protocol (OLSR) is built for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). It is a table-driven, proactive protocol: nodes exchange topology information regularly, so routes to all known destinations are available when needed. It is an optimization of the classical link-state algorithm, with three savings. Only selected nodes retransmit flooded control messages, only those nodes generate link-state information, and they may report only the links to the nodes that selected them.

OLSR is fully distributed and needs no central entity. It does not require reliable or sequenced delivery of control messages, because messages are sent periodically and carry sequence numbers, so it can tolerate the losses common in radio networks. It makes no assumption about the link layer, needs no change to the IP packet format, and only interacts with routing table management. The RFC says it is well suited to large and dense networks and to traffic that is random and sporadic between many nodes.

The specification is split into a core (packet format and forwarding, link sensing, neighbor detection, MPR selection, topology discovery and route calculation) and optional auxiliary functions: non-OLSR interfaces, link-layer notifications, link hysteresis, redundant topology information and redundant MPR flooding.
sections.plainLanguage: OLSR is a way for walkie-talkie users who keep moving around to always know the best path to reach anyone else, without a boss keeping the map.

sections.title: Multipoint Relays
sections.content:
Each node chooses a multipoint relay (MPR) set from its symmetric (bi-directional) 1-hop neighbors. The set must be chosen so that every node in the node's symmetric strict 2-hop neighborhood has a symmetric link to at least one MPR. Neighbors that are not MPRs receive and process broadcasts but do not retransmit them. A node that has chosen another as its MPR is that node's MPR selector.

The smaller the MPR set, the less control overhead. The RFC gives a heuristic: start with all neighbors of willingness WILL_ALWAYS, add neighbors that are the only route to some 2-hop node, then repeatedly add the neighbor that covers the most still-uncovered 2-hop nodes, preferring higher willingness and then higher degree. Redundant members may then be pruned. Other algorithms are allowed.

Because MPRs are only selected among symmetric neighbors, routes through them avoid the problems of sending data over uni-directional links. A node advertises its willingness to carry traffic from 0 to 7. WILL_NEVER (0) means it is never selected, for example because of low battery, and WILL_ALWAYS (7) means it is always selected. The default is WILL_DEFAULT (3).
sections.plainLanguage: Each kid in a playground picks a few friends who can reach all the kids two steps away. Only those friends repeat the message, so the news spreads without everybody yelling.

sections.title: Packets and Message Flooding
sections.content:
OLSR uses a single packet format carried in UDP, and port 698 is assigned by IANA exclusively for it. A packet has a 16-bit Packet Length and a 16-bit Packet Sequence Number, followed by one or more messages. Every message shares a header: Message Type, Vtime (how long the information stays valid), Message Size, Originator Address, Time To Live, Hop Count and Message Sequence Number. The Originator Address is never changed in retransmission. The common header lets nodes forward message types they do not understand.

Each node keeps a duplicate set so that a message is processed and retransmitted at most once. Under the default forwarding algorithm a message is retransmitted only if it came from a symmetric neighbor that is one of the node's MPR selectors and its TTL is greater than 1. Before retransmission the TTL is decremented and the hop count incremented. To avoid synchronized transmissions, nodes SHOULD add random jitter to message emission and forwarding.

The message types are HELLO (1), TC (2), MID (3) and HNA (4). Values 5 to 127 can be allocated by standards action and 128 to 255 are for private or local use.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note has a standard envelope that says who wrote it, how far it may travel and which number it is, so nobody passes the same note around twice.

sections.title: HELLO Messages and Neighbor Sensing
sections.content:
HELLO messages are sent only to the immediate neighborhood (TTL of 1) and do three jobs at once: link sensing, neighbor detection and MPR selection signaling. A HELLO carries the sender's emission interval (Htime), its willingness, and groups of neighbor interface addresses, each tagged with a Link Code made of a Link Type and a Neighbor Type.

  • Link types: UNSPEC_LINK (0), ASYM_LINK (1, heard in one direction), SYM_LINK (2, verified both ways) and LOST_LINK (3).
  • Neighbor types: NOT_NEIGH (0), SYM_NEIGH (1) and MPR_NEIGH (2, selected as MPR by the sender).

When a node sees its own address advertised as MPR_NEIGH in a neighbor's HELLO, it records that neighbor in its MPR selector set. The HELLOs also let a node learn its 2-hop neighbors. A node with several interfaces picks one address as its main address, and MID messages tie its other interface addresses to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors keep saying hi and who they can hear. From these greetings each kid learns who is close and who can really talk back.

sections.title: Topology Control and Routes
sections.content:
Nodes selected as MPRs broadcast Topology Control (TC) messages. A TC lists the node's advertised neighbors, which MUST include at least its MPR selectors, and carries an Advertised Neighbor Sequence Number (ANSN) so receivers can tell newer information from older. TC messages are flooded using the default forwarding algorithm, with the TTL set to 255 (it SHOULD be), and receivers keep the result in a topology set.

Each node computes its routing table with a shortest path algorithm over the links it knows: its symmetric neighbors, its 2-hop neighbors, and the topology tuples learned from TC messages. Entries record the destination, the next hop, the distance in hops and the local interface. The table is recalculated whenever the link, neighbor, 2-hop, topology or multiple-interface information changes, and recalculation by itself sends no messages.

Sequence number comparison is defined so that wrap-around is handled correctly. The RFC proposes defaults of a HELLO interval of 2 seconds and a TC interval of 5 seconds, with neighbor information held for 3 times the refresh interval and topology information for 3 times the TC interval.
sections.plainLanguage: The chosen friends tell everybody who they can reach. Each kid then puts these tips together into a map and always picks the path with the fewest steps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that OLSR does not specify any special security measures. As a proactive protocol it periodically reveals the network topology to anyone who listens on an unprotected wireless network. The RFC suggests ordinary cryptographic techniques such as encrypting control traffic if confidentiality matters.

For integrity, it lists problems such as nodes advertising non-neighbors, pretending to be another node, forwarding altered messages, choosing MPRs incorrectly, or replaying old control traffic. It recommends message authentication, notes that replay protection needs temporal information, and says signatures could travel in a separate message type so secured and unsecured nodes can coexist. Because every control message is point-to-multipoint, the authentication method must let any receiver validate it. Gateways to external routing domains must validate OLSR information before injecting it.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone nearby can overhear the greetings, and a prankster could lie about who they can reach. The RFC says to use secret codes or signatures if that matters, but OLSR itself does not include them.
